q: Which animal is the fastest member of the whole animal kingdom, thanks to its hunting dive?
x: When it dives on prey, a peregrine can top 300 km/h (190 mph). It is fastest going down, not in level flight.
evidence: The peregrine falcon is the fastest bird, and the fastest member of the animal kingdom, with a diving speed of over 300 km/h (190 mph).

q: Which animal is the fastest on land?
x: The cheetah's top speed reliably measured is about 104 km/h (65 mph), but it can only keep it up for short sprints.
evidence: The fastest land animal is the cheetah, capable of running at speeds of up to 93–104 km/h (58–65 mph).

q: How long does it take a cheetah to speed up from 0 to 97 km/h (60 mph)?
x: That is faster than many sports cars. When sprinting, a cheetah spends more time in the air than on the ground.
evidence: the cheetah can accelerate from 0 to 97 km/h (60 mph) in less than three seconds, "faster than a Ferrari"

q: Which animal is the fastest runner on two legs?
x: The ostrich is also the fastest bird on land. Its highest reliably measured speed is about 61 km/h (38 mph).
evidence: The ostrich is the fastest bird on land, as well as the fastest running animal on two legs.

q: Which animal is the fastest runner over long distances?
x: The North American pronghorn can run at 56 km/h (35 mph) for 6 km (3.7 mi). Cheetahs tire after a short sprint.
evidence: The pronghorn (American antelope) is the fastest animal over long distances; it can run at 56 km/h (35 mph) for 6 km (3.7 mi)

q: Which is the fastest mammal of all, reaching about 160 km/h in level flight?
x: This little bat lives in huge colonies and is one of the fastest flying animals in level flight.
evidence: Mexican free-tailed bat 160 km/h (99 mph) Flight It is the fastest mammal in the world and one of the fastest flying animals on level flight.

q: Measured in body lengths per second, what is the fastest known animal on Earth?
x: This Californian mite runs 322 body lengths per second. A human doing that would hit about 2,092 km/h (1,300 mph).
evidence: On this basis the 'fastest' organism on earth, relative to its body length, is the Southern Californian mite, Paratarsotomus macropalpis, which has a speed of 322 body lengths per second.

q: Which bird is the fastest in normal flapping flight (not diving)?
x: This swift reaches about 169 km/h (105 mph). The peregrine is fastest only when it dives.
evidence: White-throated needletail swift 169 km/h (105 mph) Flight The fastest flying bird in flapping flight.

q: Which bird holds the vertebrate record for speed in body lengths per second, at 276?
x: By comparison, a diving peregrine falcon manages about 186 body lengths per second.
evidence: Anna's hummingbird 98.27 km/h (61.06 mph) Flight The stated speed equals 276 body lengths per second, the highest known length-specific velocity attained by any vertebrate.

q: Which Australian lizard is generally considered the fastest recorded reptile?
x: The perentie, a big monitor lizard, has been clocked at about 40 km/h (25 mph).
evidence: Perentie 40.23 km/h (25.00 mph) Land Generally considered the fastest recorded reptile.

q: Which dogs are the fastest of all dogs?
x: Greyhounds can reach 60 to 70 km/h (37 to 43 mph). They were bred for chasing game and for racing.
evidence: Greyhounds are the fastest dogs, and have primarily been bred for coursing game and racing .

q: Which seabird has the largest wing area compared to its body weight of any bird?
x: Its huge wings for its light body help the frigatebird reach about 153 km/h (95 mph).
evidence: The frigatebird's high speed is helped by its having the largest wing-area-to-body-weight ratio of any bird.

q: What is the largest animal known to have ever lived?
x: Blue whales can weigh up to about 190 to 200 tonnes and reach about 30 m (98 to 100 ft) long.
evidence: Reaching a maximum confirmed length of 29.9–30.5 m (98–100 ft) and weighing up to 190–200 t (190–200 long tons; 210–220 short tons), it is the largest animal known to have ever existed.

q: What is the largest living land animal?
x: Males weigh about 6 tonnes (13,000 lb) on average and live in open habitats across sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: The African bush elephant (Loxodonta africana) is the largest living land animal.

q: About how much did the heart of a stranded blue whale weigh, the largest heart known?
x: That is the heaviest heart known in any animal. Its heart can slow to just 2 beats per minute on deep dives.
evidence: The weight of the heart of a stranded North Atlantic blue whale was 180 kg (400 lb), the largest known in any animal.

q: How slow can a blue whale's heart beat when it dives deep?
x: When the whale comes back to the surface, its heart rate can rise to about 37 beats per minute.
evidence: A blue whale's heart rate can drop to 2 beats per minute (bpm) at deep depths, but upon surfacing, can rise to 37 bpm, which is close to its peak heart rate.

q: What does the blue whale eat almost exclusively?
x: An average blue whale must eat about 1,120 kg (2,469 lb) of krill a day, which it gulps in huge lunges.
evidence: Blue whales are filter feeders; their diet consists almost exclusively of krill.

q: What is the smallest bird in the world?
x: It weighs about 1.95 g (0.069 oz) and is about 5.5 cm (2.2 in) long, the smallest warm-blooded vertebrate.
evidence: the bee hummingbird (Mellisuga helenae) is the smallest known dinosaur as well as the smallest bird species, and the smallest warm-blooded vertebrate.

q: The bee hummingbird, the world's smallest bird, is native to which island?
x: Locals call it the zunzuncito. It beats its wings 80 to 200 times per second.
evidence: The bee hummingbird, zunzuncito or Helena hummingbird (Mellisuga helenae) is a species of hummingbird, native to the island of Cuba in the Caribbean.

q: The bee hummingbird lays the tiniest eggs. Each is about the size of what?
x: The female lays only two eggs at a time. She is the smallest known bird.
evidence: The female lays only two eggs at a time, each about the size of a coffee bean.

q: Which is the smallest mammal by mass?
x: It weighs only about 1.8 g (0.063 oz) on average.
evidence: The Etruscan shrew (Suncus etruscus), is the smallest mammal by mass, weighing about 1.8 g (0.063 oz) on average.

q: The bumblebee bat, the smallest mammal by length, lives in which countries?
x: It is only 29 to 33 mm (1.1 to 1.3 in) long and weighs about 2 g (0.071 oz).
evidence: The Kitti's hog-nosed bat (Craseonycteris thonglongyai), also known as the bumblebee bat, from Thailand and Myanmar is the smallest bat and the smallest mammal by body length

q: The smallest primate in the world is a kind of what?
x: Madame Berthe's mouse lemur lives in Madagascar and is about 9.2 cm (3.6 in) long on average.
evidence: The smallest primate is Madame Berthe's mouse lemur (Microcebus berthae), found in Madagascar, with an average body length of 9.2 cm (3.6 in).

q: Which animal is the smallest member of the order Carnivora?
x: The least weasel can weigh as little as 29.5 g (1.04 oz), and females are lighter than males.
evidence: The smallest member of the order Carnivora is the least weasel (Mustela nivalis), with an average body length of 114–260 mm (4.5–10.2 in).

q: What is the smallest of all the whales, dolphins and porpoises?
x: The vaquita is a porpoise only about 1.4 m (4.6 ft) long. It is also one of the most endangered.
evidence: The smallest cetacean, which is also (as of 2006) the most endangered, is the vaquita, a species of porpoise.

q: What is the smallest species of penguin?
x: It stands only about 30 to 33 cm (12 to 13 in) tall and weighs about 1.2 to 1.3 kg (2.6 to 2.9 lb).
evidence: The smallest penguin species is the little blue penguin (Eudyptula minor), which stands around 30–33 cm (12–13 in) tall and weighs 1.2–1.3 kg (2.6–2.9 lb).

q: The smallest bird of prey, the black-thighed falconet, is roughly the size of what?
x: Its wingspan is only about 27 to 32 cm (11 to 13 in).
evidence: The smallest bird of prey is the black-thighed falconet (Microhierax fringillarius), with a wingspan of 27–32 centimetres (11–13 in), roughly the size of a sparrow.

q: The smallest known vertebrate, only about 6.5 mm long, is what kind of animal?
x: Brachycephalus pulex, a Brazilian flea toad, is also the smallest amphibian known.
evidence: The smallest vertebrate (and smallest amphibian) known is Brachycephalus pulex, a Brazilian flea toad, with a minimum adult snout–vent length of 6.45 millimetres (0.254 in).

q: Brookesia nana, possibly the smallest reptile, is what kind of lizard?
x: This tiny chameleon has a body only about 13.5 mm (0.53 in) long, without its tail.
evidence: The miniature chameleon Brookesia nana, with a snout-vent length of 13.5 mm (0.53 in), may represent the smallest known lizard and smallest reptile.

q: The world's smallest turtle, the speckled padloper tortoise, comes from which country?
x: Males are only about 6 to 8 cm (2.4 to 3.1 in) long. Females reach almost 10 cm (3.9 in).
evidence: The smallest turtle is the speckled padloper tortoise (Homopus signatus) from South Africa.

q: Which animal is the longest-lived vertebrate known?
x: One Greenland shark 5 m (16.5 ft) long was found to be between 272 and 512 years old.
evidence: That makes the Greenland shark the longest-lived vertebrate.

q: Which whales are thought to live at least 211 years, making them the oldest mammals?
x: Bowhead whales live only in Arctic and subarctic waters and use their huge skulls to break through sea ice.
evidence: Some confirmed sources estimate bowhead whales to have lived at least 211 years of age, making them the oldest mammals.

q: Which animals may be the longest-lived on Earth, estimated at over 10,000 years old?
x: These sponges live in the East China Sea and Southern Ocean. The estimate may be too high, but they are likely the longest-lived animals.
evidence: Glass sponges found in the East China Sea and Southern Ocean have been estimated to be more than 10,000 years old.

q: Wisdom, the oldest known wild bird, laid an egg at age 74. What kind of bird is she?
x: Wisdom lives on Midway Atoll in the Pacific Ocean and laid that egg in December 2024.
evidence: A female Laysan albatross named Wisdom successfully laid an egg at Midway Atoll in December 2024, at the age of 74. As of 2025, she is the oldest known wild bird in the world.

q: Cocky Bennett, the oldest known bird, lived to 120. What kind of bird was he?
x: This Australian sulphur-crested cockatoo lived from 1796 to 1916 and could say phrases like "one feather more and I'll fly".
evidence: The oldest known bird in the world was an Australian sulphur-crested cockatoo called Cocky Bennett, who lived to 120.

q: The tuatara, a lizard-like reptile that can live over 100 years, is native to which country?
x: A tuatara named Henry became a father for the first time at about 111 years old.
evidence: The tuatara, a lizard-like reptile native to New Zealand, can live well over 100 years.

q: A splendor beetle once came out of a staircase in England after how long as a larva?
x: The beetle emerged from the staircase in Essex, UK, on 27 May 1983.
evidence: On May 27, 1983, a splendor beetle emerged from a staircase in Essex, UK, after at least 47 years as a larva.

q: Which living bird is both the tallest and the heaviest?
x: Male ostriches stand up to about 2.75 m (9 ft) tall and weigh 100 to 130 kg (220 to 290 lb).
evidence: The common ostrich is the tallest and heaviest living bird.

q: Which land animal with a backbone has the biggest eyes?
x: An ostrich eye is about 50 mm (2 in) across, helping it spot predators from far away.
evidence: their eyes are the largest of any land vertebrate, 50 mm (2.0 in) in diameter, helping them to see predators at a great distance.

q: About how much does an ostrich egg weigh?
x: That is over 20 times the weight of a chicken's egg, yet small compared to the mother's body.
evidence: on average they are 15 cm (5.9 in) long, 13 cm (5.1 in) wide, and weigh 1.4 kg (3.1 lb), over 20 times the weight of a chicken's egg

q: How many toes does an ostrich have on each foot?
x: Most birds have four toes. Having fewer toes seems to help the ostrich run fast.
evidence: The bird is didactyl, having just two toes on each foot (most birds have four), with the nail on the larger, inner toe resembling a hoof.

q: Which animal has the largest eyes ever documented?
x: Its eyes are about 27 to 30 cm (11 to 12 in) across, roughly the size of a dinner plate.
evidence: The colossal squid has the largest eyes of any documented animal, with an estimated diameter of 27–30 cm (11–12 in) to 40 cm (16 in) for the largest collected specimen.

q: What is the heaviest living invertebrate (animal without a backbone)?
x: It can weigh at least 495 kg (1,091 lb). It lives in the cold Southern Ocean around Antarctica.
evidence: Unlike most squid species, the colossal squid exhibits abyssal gigantism, as it is the heaviest living invertebrate species, reaching weights up to 495 kg (1,091 lb).

q: What makes the colossal squid's arms and tentacles different from those of its close relatives?
x: Many sperm whales have scars on their backs thought to be made by these hooks.
evidence: the colossal squid is the only squid in its family whose arms and tentacles are equipped with hooks, either swiveling or three-pointed.

q: Which bird makes the longest migration known in the whole animal kingdom?
x: Birds nesting in Iceland and Greenland fly about 70,900 km (38,300 nmi) on their yearly round trip.
evidence: These are by far the longest migrations known in the animal kingdom.

q: Why does the Arctic tern see more daylight than any other creature?
a: It follows summer from pole to pole
x: It breeds in the Arctic, then flies to the Antarctic coast for the southern summer, so it sees two summers a year.
evidence: The long journey ensures that this bird sees two summers per year and more daylight than any other creature on the planet.

q: At about what age is a Greenland shark grown up enough to have babies?
x: Its pups are born alive after a pregnancy thought to last 8 to 18 years.
evidence: They reach sexual maturity around 150 years of age and their pups are born alive after an estimated gestation period of 8 to 18 years.

q: What often clings to a Greenland shark's eyes, sometimes making it nearly blind?
x: The copepod Ommatokoita elongata attaches to the eyes. The shark relies more on smell and its lateral line.
evidence: The shark is often infested by the copepod Ommatokoita elongata, a crustacean that attaches itself to the shark's eyes.

q: Where does the ocean sunfish get its English name?
x: While it basks on its side, seabirds pick parasites off its skin. Adults actually spend lots of time hunting deep down.
evidence: Its common English name, sunfish, refers to the animal's habit of sunbathing at the surface of the sea.

q: What is strange about the shape of the ocean sunfish?
a: It looks like a head with no tail
o: It is shaped like a ribbon
x: Its tail fin is replaced by a rounded flap called a clavus. In Polish its name means "head alone".
evidence: It resembles a fish head without a tail, and its main body is flattened laterally.

q: Which animal makes the loudest sounds of any animal, up to 236 decibels?
x: Sperm whales use these powerful clicks for echolocation to find squid in the dark deep sea.
evidence: The sperm whale uses echolocation and vocalization with source level as loud as 236 decibels (re 1 μPa m) underwater, the loudest of any animal.

q: Which animal has the largest brain on Earth?
x: A sperm whale's brain weighs about 7 kg (15.6 lb) on average, more than five times heavier than a human brain.
evidence: The sperm whale's brain is the largest in the world, five times heavier than a human brain.

q: Where are a sperm whale's working teeth?
x: The cone-shaped teeth can weigh up to 1 kg (2.2 lb) each and fit into sockets in the upper jaw.
evidence: The sperm whale has 18 to 26 teeth on each side of its lower jaw which fit into sockets in the upper jaw.

q: How do sperm whales sleep for short periods?
x: Pods may sleep with their heads just below or at the surface, or head down. Deep sleep is often between 6 p.m. and midnight.
evidence: For some time researchers have been aware that pods of sperm whales may sleep for short periods, assuming a vertical position with their heads just below or at the surface, or head down.

q: What is the main food of the sperm whale?
x: It eats medium-sized squid most, but also hunts giant squid, colossal squid, octopuses and fish.
evidence: They feed on several species, notably the giant squid, but also the colossal squid, octopuses, and fish such as demersal rays and sharks, but their diet is mainly medium-sized squid.

q: When a pistol shrimp snaps its claw, the collapsing bubble gives off what?
x: The snap is so powerful it can stun fish and even break small glass jars.
evidence: As it collapses, the cavitation bubble emits a short flash of light with a broad spectrum.

q: Some pistol shrimps share their burrow with which fish, which keeps watch for danger?
x: The shrimp builds and tends the burrow. The goby has better eyesight and warns the shrimp with a flick of its tail.
evidence: Some snapping shrimp species share burrows with goby fish in a mutualistic symbiotic relationship: the burrow is built and tended by the pistol shrimp, and the goby provides protection by watching out for danger.

q: How many legs does a tardigrade (water bear) have?
x: The name water bear comes from the way they walk, a bit like a bear.
evidence: Tardigrades (/ˈtɑːrdɪɡreɪdz/ ⓘ), also known as water bears or moss piglets, are a phylum of eight-legged segmented micro-animals.

q: Which tiny animals have survived being exposed to outer space?
x: In 2007 dried-out tardigrades were sent into orbit on the FOTON-M3 mission and exposed to the vacuum of space.
evidence: They have survived exposure to outer space.

q: What is the tallest living land animal?
x: Fully grown giraffes stand 4.3 to 5.7 m (14 to 19 ft) tall. They are also the largest ruminants.
evidence: They are the tallest living terrestrial animals and the largest ruminants on Earth.

q: About how long is a giraffe's tongue?
x: Giraffes use their long tongues to grab leaves from high branches.
evidence: A giraffe's tongue is about 45 cm (18 in) long.

q: Why is a giraffe's neck so long?
a: Its neck bones are extra long
x: Each neck vertebra is over 28 cm (11 in) long. Most of the stretching happens after the calf is born.
evidence: The long neck results from a disproportionate lengthening of the cervical vertebrae, not from the addition of more vertebrae.

q: A giraffe's heart must pump blood up to its brain at about what blood pressure, compared with a human?
x: Its heart weighs about 11 kg (25 lb) and its wall can be as thick as 7.5 cm (3 in).
evidence: Its 11 kg (25 lb) and 60 cm (2 ft) heart must generate approximately double the blood pressure required for a human to maintain blood flow to the brain.

q: In captivity, about how many hours a day do giraffes sleep?
x: They sleep mostly at night, usually lying down, sometimes resting the head on the hip.
evidence: Studies in captivity found that giraffes sleep intermittently around 4.6 hours per day, mostly at night.

q: Giraffes mainly eat the leaves of which kind of tree?
x: Giraffes browse at heights other ground animals cannot reach. They eat leaves, fruits and flowers.
evidence: Their food source is leaves, fruits, and flowers of woody plants, primarily acacia species, which they browse at heights most other ground-based herbivores cannot reach.

q: About how long is an African bush elephant pregnancy, the longest of any mammal?
x: Elephant herds are made up of cows and their young.
evidence: The menstrual cycle of cows lasts three to four months, and gestation around 22 months, the longest of any mammal.

q: What do an African bush elephant's huge ears mainly help it do?
x: Flapping the ears creates air currents and lets heat escape from big blood vessels inside them. Ears can be 2 m long.
evidence: Its large ears help to reduce body heat; flapping them creates air currents and exposes large blood vessels on the inner sides to increase heat loss during hot weather.

q: How many finger-like tips are at the end of an African bush elephant's trunk?
x: These tips let the elephant pick up small objects. Its tusks curve outward and point forward.
evidence: Its long trunk or proboscis ends with two finger-like tips.

q: What is the largest living reptile?
x: The very largest may reach 6 to 7 m (20 to 23 ft) long and weigh 900 to 1,500 kg (2,000 to 3,300 lb).
evidence: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile.

q: Which is the longest snake in the world?
x: It is native to South and Southeast Asia and is the only snake that regularly grows over 6 m (20 ft).
evidence: The mainland subspecies is the world's longest snake, and the third heaviest after the green anaconda and Burmese python.

q: Which is the heaviest snake in the world?
x: Typical adults weigh 30 to 80 kg (66 to 176 lb). It is the largest snake native to the Americas.
evidence: The green anaconda is the world's heaviest and one of the world's longest snakes

q: What is the largest living fish?
x: The largest reliably recorded whale shark was 18.8 m (61.7 ft) long.
evidence: The whale shark (Rhincodon typus) is a slow-moving, filter-feeding carpet shark and the largest known extant fish species.

q: What does the gigantic whale shark mainly eat?
x: It filters food with 20 filter pads. Its mouth can be over 1.5 m (5 ft) wide, with hundreds of rows of tiny teeth.
evidence: The whale shark is an active filter feeder, primarily consuming plankton, krill, fish eggs, and small schooling fish such as sardines and anchovies.

q: The goliath frog, the largest living frog, lives in which countries?
x: It lives mostly near waterfalls. With legs stretched out, the biggest ones can be over 80 cm (31 in) long.
evidence: The goliath frog is mainly found near waterfalls in Equatorial Guinea and Cameroon.

q: What is unusual about the goliath frog compared with most frogs?
o: It lays eggs on land only
x: It lacks a vocal sac, so it stays silent. Goliath frogs build nests in or near rivers.
evidence: Because the goliath frog lacks a vocal sac, it does not produce mating calls, a behavior generally present in frogs and toads.

q: Which bird has the longest wingspan of any living bird?
x: Its wings can span up to 3.7 m (12 ft), letting it glide for hours without flapping.
evidence: The snowy albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird, reaching up to 3.7 m (12 ft)

q: Which bird is considered the highest flying, once recorded at 11,300 m (37,000 ft)?
x: Special blood protein lets it absorb oxygen in thin air. That record flight ended when it hit a plane over Ivory Coast.
evidence: It is considered to be the highest-flying bird, with confirmed evidence of a flight at an altitude of 11,300 m (37,000 ft)

q: Which bird makes the longest known non-stop flight, from Alaska to New Zealand?
x: It is also the longest journey any animal makes without stopping to feed.
evidence: The migration of the subspecies Limosa lapponica baueri across the Pacific Ocean from Alaska to New Zealand is the longest known non-stop flight of any bird

q: Which mammal holds the record for the deepest dive, nearly 3,000 m (9,800 ft)?
x: It also holds the record for the longest dive by a mammal, 222 minutes.
evidence: Recorded dives have reached depths of 2,992 m (9,816 ft) and durations of 222 minutes.

q: How long can a young common swift keep flying without ever landing?
x: Swifts never land on the ground by choice. Their tiny legs are mainly for clinging to walls.
evidence: They never settle voluntarily on the ground where they would be vulnerable to accidents and predation, and non-breeding individuals may spend up to ten months in continuous flight.

q: What does the bowhead whale use its huge triangular skull for?
x: It is the only baleen whale that lives only in Arctic waters, and it may live more than 200 years.
evidence: It is the only baleen whale endemic to the Arctic and subarctic waters, and is named after its characteristic massive triangular skull, which it uses to break through Arctic ice.

q: One ocean quahog was found to have lived 507 years. What kind of animal is it?
x: It is the longest-lived single animal whose age was accurately known.
evidence: An individual specimen was reported to have lived 507 years, making it the longest-lived non-clonal metazoan whose age was accurately known.

q: Jonathan, the oldest known living land animal, is a tortoise living on which island?
x: Jonathan hatched around 1832 and was brought to Saint Helena from the Seychelles in 1882.
evidence: Jonathan lives on the grounds of the Plantation House on Saint Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean.

q: Humans have 4 types of light-sensing cells in their eyes. How many types does a mantis shrimp have?
x: Mantis shrimp can even see ultraviolet and polarised light. Each eye moves on its own stalk.
evidence: Compared with the four types of photoreceptor cell that humans possess in their eyes, the eyes of a mantis shrimp have between 12 and 16 types of photoreceptor cells.

q: When a mantis shrimp strikes, its prey gets hit twice. What causes the second hit?
x: The claw strikes so fast it makes a vapour bubble, and the shock wave alone can stun or kill prey.
evidence: which means that the prey is hit twice by a single strike; first by the claw and then by the collapsing cavitation bubbles that immediately follow.

q: The animal with the most legs on Earth, with up to 1,306, is a kind of what?
x: It was found 60 m underground in drill holes in Western Australia. It was the first millipede found with over 1,000 legs.
evidence: This millipede can have as many as 1,306 legs, which makes this species the animal with the most legs on Earth and the first millipede discovered to have 1,000 legs or more.

q: Which animal has the largest leg span of any arthropod, about 3.75 m (12.3 ft)?
x: Its Japanese name, taka-ashi-gani, means "tall-legged crab".
evidence: At around 3.75 metres (12.3 ft), it has the largest leg-span of any arthropod.

q: What is the largest living lizard?
x: Males can grow to 3 m (10 ft) long and weigh up to 150 kg (330 lb).
evidence: It is the largest extant species of lizard, with the males growing to a maximum length of 3 m (10 ft) and weighing up to 150 kg (330 lb).

q: Wild Komodo dragons live only on a few islands in which country?
x: They live on Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Dasami and Gili Motang. Fossils show they once lived in Australia too.
evidence: is endemic to the Indonesian islands of Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Dasami, and Gili Motang.

q: What does a Komodo dragon mainly use to smell and taste the air?
x: Like snakes, it flicks its long yellow tongue and uses a special organ in its mouth called the Jacobson's organ.
evidence: the Komodo dragon primarily relies on its tongue to detect, taste, and smell stimuli, with the vomeronasal sense using the Jacobson's organ, rather than using the nostrils.

q: Where do young Komodo dragons live to stay safe from predators, including adult dragons?
x: Young dragons climb well with their strong claws and eat insects, birds, eggs and small reptiles.
evidence: Young Komodo dragons are vulnerable and dwell in trees to avoid predators, including cannibalistic adults

q: What is the largest of all living turtles?
x: It can reach 2.7 m (8 ft 10 in) long and 500 kg (1,100 lb). It can dive as deep as 1,280 m (4,200 ft).
evidence: The largest of all living turtles and the heaviest non-crocodilian reptile, it reaches lengths of up to 2.7 metres (8 ft 10 in) and weights of 500 kilograms (1,100 lb).

q: What makes the leatherback different from all other modern sea turtles?
x: Its back is covered by oily flesh and flexible, leather-like skin, which gives it its name.
evidence: It can easily be differentiated from other modern sea turtles by its lack of a bony shell; instead, its carapace is covered by oily flesh and flexible, leather-like skin, for which it is named.

q: What do adult leatherback sea turtles eat almost entirely?
x: Leatherbacks follow jellyfish up and down through the water, so they help keep jellyfish numbers in check.
evidence: Adult D. coriacea turtles subsist almost entirely on jellyfish.

q: What is the largest living rodent?
x: The capybara is a semiaquatic herbivore that lives near rivers, lakes and swamps.
evidence: The capybara (/kæpɪˈbɑːrə/ ⓘ kap-ih-BAR-uh) or greater capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) is the largest living rodent, native to all countries in South America except Chile.

q: Capybaras live wild in every South American country except one. Which?
x: Capybaras are semiaquatic and live near rivers, lakes, ponds, swamps and reservoirs.
evidence: Capybaras are found in all countries in South America except Chile.

q: Which is the tallest and heaviest of all living penguins?
x: Adults are about 1 m (39 in) long and weigh 22 to 45 kg (49 to 99 lb). They live only in Antarctica.
evidence: The emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) is the tallest and heaviest of all living penguin species and is endemic to Antarctica.

q: Who keeps the emperor penguin's egg warm through the Antarctic winter?
x: He balances the egg on his feet under a fold of skin for 65 to 75 days and eats nothing, losing about 12 kg (26 lb).
evidence: There he balances it on the tops of his feet, engulfing it with loose skin and feathers for around 65–75 days until hatching.

q: How do male emperor penguins survive winter winds of up to 200 km/h?
a: They huddle and take turns in the middle
x: A huddle can hold from ten to several hundred birds, each leaning on a neighbour.
evidence: To survive the cold and savage winds of up to 200 km/h (120 mph), the males huddle together, taking turns in the middle of the huddle.

q: Why is Turritopsis dohrnii called the immortal jellyfish?
a: It can turn back into a young polyp
x: After becoming an adult, it can go back to an early polyp stage attached to the sea floor and start its life again.
evidence: It is one of the few known cases of an animal capable of completely reverting to a sexually immature, sedentary polyps colonial stage after having reached sexual maturity as a solitary individual.

q: The tentacles of a large lion's mane jellyfish can trail how far?
x: It is one of the largest known jellyfish. Its trailing tentacles look a bit like a lion's mane.
evidence: The tentacles of larger specimens may trail as long as 30 m (100 ft) or more

q: What do adult mayflies eat?
x: Adults only live to breed. Their mouthparts do not work and their gut is filled with air. Young mayflies can live years in water.
evidence: The primary function of the adult is reproduction; adults do not feed and have only vestigial mouthparts, while their digestive systems are filled with air.

q: Mayflies are the only insects that do what?
x: The winged subimago moults once more into the full adult, sometimes after only a few minutes.
evidence: the subimago moults to the full adult form, making mayflies the only insects where a winged form undergoes a further moult.

q: How many eyes does a box jellyfish have in total?
x: Some of its eyes have retinas, corneas and lenses, unusual for a jellyfish. It is also a fast, strong swimmer.
evidence: In total, the box jellyfish have six eyes on each of their four rhopalia, creating a total of 24 eyes.

q: Which snake is widely regarded as the most venomous in the world?
x: It lives in semi-arid central eastern Australia. One bite may hold enough venom to kill over 100 adult humans.
evidence: Based on the median lethal dose (LD50) of its venom in laboratory mice, the inland taipan is widely regarded as the most venomous snake in the world

q: How does the inland taipan's head change colour with the seasons?
a: Black in winter, brown in summer
o: White in winter, green in summer
x: A darker head may help it soak up heat while poking just its head out of a burrow.
evidence: The rounded snout, head and neck are usually noticeably darker than the body – glossy black in winter and dark brown in summer.

q: Which small animal is considered the most poisonous animal on the planet?
x: One wild frog carries about 1 mg of poison, enough to kill 10 to 20 humans. It lives in the rainforests of Colombia.
evidence: Despite its small size, this frog is considered to be the most poisonous extant animal species on the planet.

q: Why are golden poison frogs raised in captivity not poisonous?
a: Their poison comes from wild food
x: In the wild they eat small ants and other insects that let them make their poison.
evidence: frogs kept in captivity fed on commercially available feeder insects will eventually lose their toxicity, and frogs bred in captivity are considered non-toxic.

q: What is the world's smallest monkey?
x: It weighs just over 100 g (3.5 oz) and lives in the western Amazon rainforest. It can turn its head 180°.
evidence: The pygmy marmoset is the world's smallest monkey.

q: What is the main food of the pygmy marmoset?
x: It uses special front teeth to gouge holes in trees and make the sap flow.
evidence: The dental morphology is adapted to feeding on gum, with specialised incisors that are used to gouge trees and stimulate sap flow.

q: What is the largest living land arthropod?
x: It can weigh up to 4.1 kg (9 lb). It is a giant hermit crab that lives on islands in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
evidence: It is the largest living terrestrial arthropod, with a weight up to 4.1 kg (9.0 lb).

q: What happens if an adult coconut crab stays underwater too long?
x: Adults breathe with special lungs instead of gills. Young ones carry snail shells like other hermit crabs.
evidence: After the juvenile stage, they will drown if immersed in water for too long.

q: Which is the largest spider in the world by mass?
x: It can weigh up to 175 g (6.2 oz). Despite its name, it rarely eats birds.
evidence: Found in northern South America, it is the largest spider in the world by mass (175 g (6.2 oz)) and body length (up to 13 cm (5.1 in)), and second to the giant huntsman spider by leg span.

q: The giant huntsman spider, the largest spider by leg span, is found in which country?
x: Its legs can span up to 30 cm (1 ft) and twist forward like a crab's.
evidence: The giant huntsman spider (Heteropoda maxima) is a species of the huntsman spider family Sparassidae found in Laos.

q: In Cantonese, the Atlas moth is called the "snake's head moth". Why?
a: Its wing tips look like snake heads
x: Its wingspan is often 25 to 30 cm (10 to 12 in), making it one of the largest moths.
evidence: The Cantonese name translates to "snake's head moth", referring to the prominent extension of the forewing that resembles the head of a snake.

q: What is the largest butterfly in the world?
x: Females can have wings over 25 cm (10 in) across. It lives only in forests of Papua New Guinea.
evidence: Ornithoptera alexandrae, the Queen Alexandra's birdwing, is the largest species of butterfly in the world

q: The world's smallest known insects, called fairyflies, are really tiny what?
x: The smallest known insect is a fairyfly only 0.139 mm long, smaller than some single-celled creatures.
evidence: The Mymaridae, commonly known as fairyflies or fairy bees, are a family of chalcid wasps found in temperate, subtropical, and tropical regions throughout the world.

q: Which fish has been caught nearly 8,000 m deep, maybe a record for a fish caught on the seafloor?
x: This pale, tadpole-like fish lives in the Mariana Trench and eats tiny crustaceans.
evidence: It is known from a depth range of 6,198–8,076 m (20,335–26,496 ft), including a capture at 7,966 m (26,135 ft), which is possibly the record for a fish caught on the seafloor.

q: Which animal is the largest member of the order Carnivora?
x: Adult bulls can weigh 3,000 to 3,700 kg (6,600 to 8,200 lb), more than twice a male walrus.
evidence: It is the largest member of the clade Pinnipedia and the order Carnivora, as well as the largest extant marine mammal that is not a cetacean.

q: What does a male elephant seal use its trunk-like nose for?
x: The big nose, called a proboscis, plus their huge size, gives elephant seals their name.
evidence: It gets its name from its massive size and the large proboscis of the adult male, which is used to produce very loud roars, especially during the breeding season.

q: What is the largest land carnivore?
x: Adult males weigh 300 to 800 kg (660 to 1,760 lb). It is also the largest kind of bear.
evidence: The polar bear is the largest extant species of bear and land carnivore by body mass, with adult males weighing 300–800 kg (660–1,760 lb).

q: What colour is a polar bear's skin under its fur?
x: Its fur is white or yellowish, and it has a thick layer of fat under the skin.
evidence: The polar bear is white or yellowish-furred with black skin and a thick layer of fat.

q: What is the polar bear's main prey?
x: It mostly eats the seals' energy-rich blubber and often waits at breathing holes in the ice. Penguins live at the other pole.
evidence: They are mostly carnivorous and specialized for preying on seals, particularly ringed seals.

q: What is the largest living primate?
x: Gorillas can weigh up to 227 kg (500 lb) and have arm spans up to 2.6 m (8 ft 6 in).
evidence: Gorillas are the largest living primates, reaching heights between 1.25 and 1.8 m (4 ft 1 in and 5 ft 11 in), weights between 68 and 227 kg (150 and 500 lb), and arm spans up to 2.6 m (8 ft 6 in), depending on species and sex.

q: What do gorillas build each night to sleep in?
x: Most nests are on the ground, but smaller gorillas often prefer tree nests.
evidence: For sleep during the night, gorillas, like other great apes, build a shelter called a nest.

q: How do tigers usually live?
x: A tiger defends its home range from others of the same sex. Cubs stay with their mother for about two years.
evidence: It lives a mostly solitary life and defends its home range from individuals of the same sex.

q: What mark does a tiger have on the back of each ear?
a: A white spot ringed with black
o: A black stripe down the middle
x: Tigers have round ears and round pupils, and black, mostly vertical stripes.
evidence: On the back of the ears, it has a prominent white spot, which is surrounded by black.

q: How long can a frilled shark's pregnancy last?
x: It is called a living fossil because of its eel-like body. Its jaws hold 300 needle-like teeth.
evidence: the gestation period of the frilled shark can be up to 3.5 years long, to produce a litter of 2–15 shark pups.

q: Electric eels can deliver shocks of up to about how many volts?
x: They use the shocks to stun prey. They are nocturnal and must breathe air.
evidence: They are known for their ability to stun their prey by generating electricity, delivering shocks at up to 860 volts.

q: What kind of fish is an electric eel, despite its name?
x: Electric eels belong to the South American knifefishes, most of which only make weak electric fields.
evidence: Despite their name, electric eels are not closely related to the true eels (Anguilliformes) but are members of the electroreceptive knifefish order Gymnotiformes.

q: Some fleas can jump 50 times their body length. Which insects are even better jumpers?
x: Fleas have no wings, but their back legs are built for leaping.
evidence: Some species can leap 50 times their body length, a feat second only to jumps made by another group of insects, the superfamily of froghoppers.

q: What do adult fleas feed on?
x: Their mouthparts pierce skin and suck blood. Fleas are tiny, only 1.5 to 3.3 mm long.
evidence: Fleas live by ingesting the blood of their hosts.

q: About how many tiny lenses (ommatidia) make up each of an adult dragonfly's eyes?
x: The two big compound eyes cover most of a dragonfly's head, perfect for catching prey in midair.
evidence: An adult dragonfly's compound eyes have nearly 24,000 ommatidia each.

q: Where do young dragonflies (nymphs) live?
x: The water stage can last up to five years in some species, but most adults live five weeks or less.
evidence: Dragonflies are predatory insects, both in their aquatic nymphal stage (also known as "naiads") and as adults.

q: Which bird is generally considered the largest bird of prey in the world?
x: It has a wingspan up to 3.3 m (10 ft 10 in) and can live over 70 years.
evidence: With a maximum wingspan of 3.3 m (10 ft 10 in) and weight of 15 kg (33 lb), the Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds in the world, and is generally considered to be the largest bird of prey in the world.

q: What does the Andean condor mainly feed on?
x: It is a scavenger and likes open areas where it can spot carrion from the air.
evidence: The condor is primarily a scavenger, feeding on carrion.

q: Along with monkeys, which animals are main prey of the harpy eagle?
x: Harpy eagles hunt in the rainforest canopy and have the largest talons of any living eagle.
evidence: Along with sloths, monkeys, such as the tufted capuchin (Cebus appella), are one of the main prey of the harpy eagle

q: In the wild, hummingbirds live only in which part of the world?
x: They range from south central Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, including the Caribbean.
evidence: Hummingbirds are restricted to the Americas from south-central Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, including the Caribbean.

q: What do hummingbirds do at night to save energy?
x: In torpor they can slow their metabolism to one fifteenth of its normal rate.
evidence: To conserve energy when food is scarce and at night when not foraging, they can enter torpor, a state similar to hibernation, and slow their metabolic rate to 1⁄15 of its normal rate.

q: How do hummingbirds move along a branch?
x: Their legs are short, and in flight their feet tuck under the body.
evidence: Hummingbirds do not walk on the ground or hop like most birds, but rather shuffle laterally and use their feet to grip while perching

q: What is a male narwhal's long spiral tusk?
x: The tusk is a left canine tooth that grows 1.5 to 3 m (4.9 to 9.8 ft) long.
evidence: Males of this species have a spiralled tusk, which is a protruding left canine, that is 1.5–3.0 m (4.9–9.8 ft) long

q: What is the reddish "blood sweat" on a hippo's skin?
x: The secretion starts colourless and turns red-orange within minutes. It also stops germs from growing.
evidence: Their skin secretes a natural, red-coloured sunscreen substance that is sometimes referred to as "blood sweat" but is neither blood nor sweat.

q: How do hippos usually move around in water?
a: Walking or bouncing on the bottom
x: Their dense bones let them sink. An adult must come up to breathe at least every six minutes.
evidence: They move in the water by walking or bouncing off the bottom, rarely entering deep water.

q: When hippos leave the water at dusk, what do they go to eat?
x: Hippos stay cool in water or mud during the day. They are the third-largest land mammals.
evidence: During the day, hippos remain cool by staying in water or mud, emerging at dusk to graze on grasses.

q: Which is the largest octopus species?
x: Adults usually weigh about 15 kg (33 lb) with an arm span up to 4.3 m (14 ft).
evidence: It is the largest octopus species.

q: What makes a beaver's front teeth orange?
x: The thick, iron-rich enamel makes the chisel-like teeth strong for chewing down trees.
evidence: The incisors are covered in a thick enamel that is colored orange or reddish-brown by iron compounds.

q: Why does a beaver slap the water with its tail?
x: Others then escape into the lodge or deeper water. An adult's slap works better than a young beaver's.
evidence: Tail slaps, which involve a beaver hitting the water surface with its tail, serve as alarm signals warning other beavers of a potential threat.

q: What do beavers eat?
x: Beavers are herbivores. They eat tree bark, water plants, grasses and sedges.
evidence: They are herbivorous, consuming tree bark, aquatic plants, grasses and sedges.

q: Which bird builds the largest tree nests ever recorded, up to 1 tonne in weight?
x: Its nests can be up to 4 m (13 ft) deep and 2.5 m (8.2 ft) wide.
evidence: It builds the largest nest of any North American bird and the largest tree nests ever recorded for any animal species, up to 4 m (13 ft) deep, 2.5 m (8.2 ft) wide, and 1 metric ton (1.1 short tons) in weight.

q: What does the bald eagle mainly eat?
x: It swoops down and snatches fish from the water with its talons.
evidence: The bald eagle is an opportunistic feeder that subsists mainly on fish, upon which it swoops down and snatches from the water with its talons.

q: What is special about the nests of the sociable weaver?
x: These community nests are perhaps the most spectacular structures built by any bird. It lives in southern Africa.
evidence: The species builds large, compound, community nests, a rarity among birds.

q: Each autumn, eastern North American monarch butterflies migrate south to where?
x: They fly thousands of miles south. The return trip north in spring takes several generations.
evidence: The eastern North American monarch population is notable for its annual southward late-summer/autumn instinctive migration from the northern and central United States and southern Canada to Florida and Mexico.

q: What do monarch caterpillars feed on?
x: Eating milkweed helps protect monarchs from predators.
evidence: The larva or caterpillar eats its egg case and begins to feed on milkweed in a circular motion, often leaving a characteristic, arc-shaped hole in the leaf.

q: Periodical cicadas spend about 99.5% of their lives where?
x: The nymphs come out together in their 13th or 17th year, in huge numbers.
evidence: Magicicada species spend around 99.5% of their lives underground in an immature state called a nymph.

q: What do periodical cicada nymphs feed on while underground?
x: They suck the xylem sap from roots of broadleaf trees in the eastern United States.
evidence: While underground, the nymphs feed on xylem fluids from the roots of broadleaf forest trees in the eastern United States.

q: A kiwi egg can weigh up to about what share of the mother's body weight?
x: That is one of the largest eggs for body size of any bird. An ostrich egg is only 1 to 4% of the mother's size.
evidence: Kiwi eggs are one of the largest in proportion to body size (up to 20% of the female's weight) of any order of bird in the world.

q: Where are a kiwi's nostrils?
a: At the tip of its beak
o: At the base of its beak
x: Kiwi sniff out prey in the ground with their long beaks, often before they can see it.
evidence: using their nostrils at the end of their long beak to detect prey before they see it

q: About how long is the dwarf lanternshark, the smallest shark in the world?
x: Like its relatives, it can make light with special organs called photophores.
evidence: is the smallest shark in the world, reaching a maximum known length of 20 cm (8 in).

q: About how many bats live in Bracken Cave, Texas, the largest known bat colony?
x: These Mexican free-tailed bats fly out to feed on insects at heights of up to 3,000 m (9,800 ft).
evidence: The largest known colony is found at Bracken Cave, north of San Antonio, Texas, with nearly 20 million bats

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
x: One main heart pumps blood around the body, and two smaller hearts pump it through the gills.
evidence: They have three hearts; a systemic or main heart that circulates blood around the body and two branchial or gill hearts that pump it through the two gills.

q: Octopus blood carries oxygen using a protein rich in which metal?
x: This copper protein, haemocyanin, is different from the iron-based haemoglobin in human blood.
evidence: Octopus blood contains the copper-rich protein haemocyanin to transport oxygen.

q: Where are about two thirds of an octopus's neurons?
x: This lets each arm act with some independence. An octopus has over 500 million neurons, about as many as a dog.
evidence: Two-thirds of the neurons are in the nerve cords of its arms.

q: How can an octopus taste things?
x: Its suction cups have chemical sensors, so it can taste whatever it touches.
evidence: Their suction cups are equipped with chemoreceptors so they can taste what they touch.

q: The mimic octopus can pretend to be which dangerous animals?
x: It combines its flexible body with colour changes to copy animals predators avoid, such as lionfish, sea snakes and eels.
evidence: Some octopuses, such as the mimic octopus, can combine their flexible bodies with their colour-changing ability to mimic other, more dangerous animals, such as lionfish, sea snakes, and eels.

q: What does the veined octopus collect to build itself a shelter?
x: It even "stilt walks" while carrying stacked shells. This is an example of tool use.
evidence: The veined octopus collects discarded coconut shells, then uses them to build a shelter, an example of tool use.

q: How many compartments does a cow's stomach have?
x: They are the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. The rumen is the biggest.
evidence: Cattle have one large stomach with four compartments; the rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum.

q: About how wide is a cow's field of view?
x: Cattle get almost half their information by sight. Their eyes on the sides of the head let them see nearly all around.
evidence: This gives them a field of view of 330°, but limits binocular vision (and therefore stereopsis) to some 30° to 50°, compared to 140° in humans.

q: When cows first eat, what do they do with their food?
x: Later they bring it back up a mouthful at a time and chew it as cud before swallowing again.
evidence: While feeding, cows swallow their food without chewing; it goes into the rumen for storage.

q: What is a shark's skeleton made of?
x: Cartilage is flexible and tough, but only about half as dense as bone.
evidence: Sharks and other cartilaginous fish (skates and rays) have skeletons made of cartilage and connective tissue.

q: Some sharks lose how many teeth during their lifetime?
x: New rows of teeth move forward like a conveyor belt to replace lost ones.
evidence: Multiple rows of replacement teeth grow in a groove on the inside of the jaw and steadily move forward like a conveyor belt; some sharks lose 30,000 or more teeth in their lifetime.

q: Unlike bony fish, sharks do not have which body part?
x: Sand tiger sharks store air in their stomachs and use it a bit like a swim bladder.
evidence: Unlike bony fish, sharks do not have gas-filled swim bladders for buoyancy.

q: Sharks can find prey hidden in sand by sensing what?
x: Special organs called ampullae of Lorenzini pick up the tiny electric fields all living things produce.
evidence: Sharks find prey hidden in sand by detecting the electric fields they produce.

q: Why is a snake's tongue forked?
a: To tell which way a smell comes from
o: To catch flies in the air
x: The tongue gathers particles and carries them to the Jacobson's organ in the mouth.
evidence: The forked structure of the tongue provides directional information of smell which helps locate prey or predators.

q: Why can't snakes blink?
a: Their eyelids are clear fixed scales
x: These clear scales are called spectacles or brille, and they stay closed all the time.
evidence: The eyelids of a snake are transparent "spectacle" scales, also known as brille, which remain permanently closed.

q: Which of these islands has no native snakes?
x: Snakes live on every continent except Antarctica, but not in Ireland, Iceland, Greenland or New Zealand.
evidence: exceptions include Ireland, Iceland, Greenland and the islands of New Zealand, as well as many small islands of the Atlantic and Central Pacific oceans.

q: Owls can turn their heads up to about how far?
x: Owls have 14 neck vertebrae, twice as many as humans, and special blood vessels so the brain keeps its blood supply.
evidence: Owls can rotate their heads and necks as much as 270°.

q: What does the flat disc of feathers on an owl's face do?
x: In many owls the ears are placed unevenly, which helps them pinpoint exactly where a sound comes from.
evidence: The feathers making up this disc can be adjusted to sharply focus sounds from varying distances onto the owls' asymmetrically placed ear cavities.

q: Where are a starfish's eyes?
a: At the tips of its arms
o: In the middle of its back
x: Each eyespot is made of 80 to 200 simple light-sensing ocelli.
evidence: There are eyespots at the ends of the arms, each one made of 80–200 simple ocelli composed of pigmented epithelial cells.

q: Most starfish have five arms. How many arms can the Antarctic starfish Labidiaster annulatus have?
x: Some starfish have six or seven arms and others 10 to 15. Most can regrow lost arms.
evidence: In Antarctic Labidiaster annulatus, the number of arms can exceed fifty.

q: Besides bats and toothed whales, which animals can echolocate?
x: These two groups of birds live in caves. Shrews also use a simple form of echolocation.
evidence: A few bird species in two cave-dwelling bird groups echolocate, namely cave swiftlets and the oilbird.

q: The spotted bat hunts moths with a call of 12.7 kHz. Why such a low pitch?
o: It is the only sound it can make
x: Many moths can hear bats, so a call below their hearing range lets this bat sneak up on them.
evidence: Euderma maculatum, a bat species that feeds on moths, uses a particularly low frequency of 12.7 kHz that cannot be heard by moths.

q: How does a platypus find prey underwater with its eyes, ears and nostrils shut?
x: It will even react to an artificial shrimp if a small electric current runs through it.
evidence: Like other monotremes, the platypus has a sense of electrolocation, which it uses to detect prey in water while its eyes, ears and nostrils are closed.

q: Where does a male platypus carry its venom?
a: In spurs on its back feet
o: In a sting on its tail
x: It is one of the few venomous mammals, and the venom is extremely painful.
evidence: It is one of the few species of venomous mammals, as the male platypus has a spur on each hind foot that delivers an extremely painful venom.

q: What does a platypus do under ultraviolet light?
x: This biofluorescence may help camouflage it from predators that can see UV light.
evidence: It is also biofluorescent and glows cyan and green when under ultraviolet light

q: Which body part does the platypus lack?
x: It is missing the genes needed to make stomach digestive enzymes. Adults also have no teeth, just grinding pads.
evidence: The platypus lacks a functional stomach, due to the lack of genes necessary for creating and secreting pepsin proteases.

q: Where does the platypus live in the wild?
x: It lives in eastern Australia, including Tasmania, and digs burrows into riverbanks.
evidence: is a semiaquatic, egg-laying mammal endemic to eastern Australia, including Tasmania.

q: What does a platypus eat?
x: The platypus is a carnivore. It probes along the bottom of streams for insect larvae, worms, crayfish and tadpoles.
evidence: The platypus is a carnivore and forages by probing along the bottom. It feeds on insect larvae, annelid worms, shrimp, crayfish, bivalves, tadpoles and fish eggs.

q: Besides camouflage, why do chameleons most often change colour?
x: A darker colour absorbs heat, while a lighter one reflects it. Colour also shows mood to other chameleons.
evidence: Colour change in chameleons has functions in camouflage, but most commonly in social signalling and reactions to temperature and other conditions.

q: How does a chameleon change its skin colour?
a: By moving tiny crystals in its skin
x: Changing the spacing of guanine crystals alters which colours of light the skin reflects.
evidence: The skin colour shifts as the chameleon is able to actively "excite" these crystals, changing the spacing between them, and this then affects which wavelengths of light are reflected and which are absorbed.

q: What is special about a chameleon's eyes?
x: Its brain handles two separate images at once. When hunting, both eyes focus forward together.
evidence: Chameleons' eyes are independently mobile, and because of this the chameleon's brain is constantly analyzing two separate, individual images of its environment.

q: About half of all chameleon species live only on which island?
x: Most chameleons live in Africa. Just one species lives in southern Europe.
evidence: with the vast majority occurring in Africa (about half of the species are restricted to Madagascar), but with a single species in southern Europe

q: Why are axolotls so useful to scientists?
a: They can regrow lost body parts
o: They can see in the dark
x: They can regrow limbs, gills and even parts of their eyes and brains.
evidence: specimens used extensively in scientific research because of their unusual ability to regenerate body parts, including limbs, gills and parts of their eyes and brains.

q: What is unusual about grown-up axolotls compared with most salamanders?
x: This is called neoteny. Axolotls become adults without changing form and stay in water all their lives.
evidence: Unlike most salamander species, axolotls retain their external gills when they mature into adulthood.

q: Wild axolotls come from lakes in the area of which city?
x: They lived in lakes such as Xochimilco and Chalco. Most of their old habitat is now covered by the city.
evidence: The desiccation of these lakes, initiated by the Aztecs and accelerated during the 20th century, has led to the destruction of much of the axolotl's natural habitat, an area now largely occupied by Mexico City.

q: What is a bottlenose dolphin's "signature whistle"?
a: A whistle unique to each dolphin
x: A dolphin develops its whistle in its first year and keeps it for life. Dolphins call each other by copying these whistles.
evidence: Bottlenose dolphins have been found to have signature whistles, a whistle that is unique to a specific individual.

q: How do dolphins usually sleep?
a: With one half of the brain at a time
x: Keeping half the brain awake lets them keep breathing and watch out for predators.
evidence: Generally, dolphins sleep with only one brain hemisphere in slow-wave sleep at a time, thus maintaining enough consciousness to breathe and to watch for possible predators and other threats.

q: Some dolphins in Australia cover their snouts with what while searching the sea floor for food?
x: The sponge protects the snout. Mothers teach this tool use to their young.
evidence: They cover their snouts with sponges to protect them while foraging.

q: What does a honey bee's waggle dance tell other bees?
a: The direction and distance to food
o: That it is time to sleep
x: Bees also use it to point the way to water and new nest sites. Karl von Frisch won a Nobel Prize for decoding it.
evidence: By performing this dance, successful foragers can share information about the direction and distance to patches of flowers yielding nectar and pollen, to water sources, or to new nest-site locations with other members of the colony.

q: In the waggle dance, what does waggling straight up the honeycomb mean?
x: The angle of the dance shows the direction, and the length of the waggle part shows the distance.
evidence: if it moves vertically the direction to the source is directly towards the Sun.

q: What do leafcutter ants do with the leaves they carry home?
x: They farm the fungus for food. A worker can carry up to 50 times its own body weight.
evidence: Leafcutter ants are several species of fungus-growing ants that share the behaviour of cutting leaves which they carry back to their nests to farm fungus.

q: Where does the common cuckoo lay its eggs?
o: In holes it digs in trees
x: It is a brood parasite. Hosts include dunnocks, meadow pipits and reed warblers, and its eggs often look like theirs.
evidence: It is a brood parasite, which means it lays eggs in the nests of other bird species, particularly of dunnocks, meadow pipits, and reed warblers.

q: What does a newly hatched cuckoo chick do to the other eggs in its nest?
x: The cuckoo chick often hatches first, so it can get rid of the unhatched eggs and get all the food.
evidence: Hatched cuckoo chicks push host eggs out of the nest.

q: An adult cuckoo looks like which bird of prey, giving the female time to lay her eggs?
x: Small birds are wary of sparrowhawks, so they hesitate to attack the cuckoo near their nests.
evidence: The adult too is a mimic, in its case of the sparrowhawk; since that species is a predator, the mimicry gives the female time to lay her eggs without being attacked.

q: Which primate was the first found to hibernate, sleeping in tree holes for seven months a year?
x: Before this discovery in Madagascar, no primate or tropical mammal was known to hibernate.
evidence: no primate or tropical mammal was known to hibernate until the discovery of hibernation in the fat-tailed dwarf lemur of Madagascar, which hibernates in tree holes for seven months of the year.

q: Which hibernating animal can let its belly temperature fall below freezing, to minus 2.9 °C?
x: It can keep a sub-zero belly temperature for more than three weeks, while its head stays at 0 °C or above.
evidence: Hibernating Arctic ground squirrels may exhibit abdominal temperatures as low as −2.9 °C (26.8 °F), maintaining sub-zero abdominal temperatures for more than three weeks at a time

q: In a lion pride, who usually does the hunting?
x: A pride is made of related females and cubs, with one or a few adult males.
evidence: Groups of female lions usually hunt together.

q: Outside Africa, which country still has wild lions?
x: The Asiatic lion survives only in and around Gir National Park in Gujarat, western India.
evidence: The Asiatic lion now survives only in and around Gir National Park in Gujarat, western India.

q: Which of these is a reason wolves howl?
a: To gather the pack before a hunt
o: To scare prey out of hiding
x: Wolves also howl to sound an alarm, find each other in storms and talk across long distances.
evidence: Wolves howl to assemble the pack usually before and after hunts, to pass on an alarm particularly at a den site, to locate each other during a storm, while crossing unfamiliar territory, and to communicate across great distances.

q: A meerkat burrow system usually has about how many entrances?
x: The burrows are about 5 m (16 ft) across with two or three levels of tunnels, staying comfy in hot and cold weather.
evidence: The burrow systems, typically 5 m (16 ft) in diameter with around 15 openings, are large underground networks consisting of two to three levels of tunnels.

q: In the wild, meerkats live in which part of the world?
x: The meerkat is a small mongoose. It lives in stony areas and big burrows in the plains, such as the Kalahari.
evidence: The meerkat (Suricata suricatta) or suricate is a small mongoose found in southern Africa.

q: How does the New Caledonian crow get grubs out of holes in wood?
a: It pokes them with a twig
o: It drums to scare them out
x: The grub bites the twig and gets pulled out. These crows can even make hooks.
evidence: The New Caledonian crow sometimes captures grubs in nooks or crevices by poking a twig at the grub to agitate it into biting the twig, which the crow then withdraws with the grub still attached.

q: Which animal has the densest fur in the animal kingdom?
x: It has up to 150,000 hairs per square centimetre. Unlike most sea mammals, it has no blubber, so its fur keeps it warm.
evidence: With up to 150,000 strands of hair per square centimetre (970,000/in2), its fur is the densest of any animal.

q: What does a sea otter use rocks for?
x: It is one of the few mammals that uses tools. It may pound prey against a rock on its chest.
evidence: Its use of rocks to dislodge prey and to open shells makes it one of the few mammal species to use tools.

q: Where does a sea otter keep food it collects, and sometimes a favourite rock?
a: In a skin pouch under its foreleg
o: In a pocket on its tail
Under a rock on the sea floor
x: It prefers the left pouch. The pouch lets it bring food up to the surface to eat.
evidence: In this pouch (preferentially the left one), the animal stores collected food to bring to the surface, and sometimes a rock that is used to break open shellfish and clams.

q: Sea otters protect kelp forests by eating lots of which animal?
x: Without sea otters, sea urchins can badly damage kelp forests, which is why the otter is called a keystone species.
evidence: In most of its range, it is a keystone species, controlling sea urchin populations which would otherwise inflict extensive damage to kelp forest ecosystems.

q: Chimpanzees use modified sticks and grass to get which of these foods?
x: Nearly all chimp groups use tools, also for honey, nuts and water.
evidence: Nearly all chimpanzee populations have been recorded using tools, modifying sticks, rocks, grass and leaves and using them for hunting and acquiring honey, termites, ants, nuts and water.

q: What does a male bowerbird build to attract a mate?
x: He decorates his bower with sticks and brightly coloured objects. Females are drab and choose the best display.
evidence: They are renowned for their unique courtship behaviour, where males build a structure and decorate it with sticks and brightly coloured objects in an attempt to attract a mate.

q: Bowerbirds live in the wild in which region?
x: Ten species live only in New Guinea, eight only in Australia, and two in both.
evidence: The bowerbirds have an Australo-Papuan distribution, with ten species endemic to New Guinea, eight endemic to Australia, and two found in both.

q: What do termites mainly eat?
x: Termites are important recyclers of dead plant matter, helped by tiny microbes in their guts.
evidence: Termites are a group of eusocial insects which consume a variety of decaying plant material, generally in the form of wood, leaf litter, and soil humus.

q: Unlike most ant colonies, how do most termite colonies begin?
a: With a king and queen pair
x: The king and queen stay together as a pair for life.
evidence: Unlike ants, most colonies begin from sexually mature individuals known as the "king" and "queen" that together form a lifelong monogamous pair.

q: Unlike most ants, what do army ants not build?
x: An army ant colony moves almost all the time. Its workers are usually blind.
evidence: unlike most ant species, army ants do not construct permanent nests; an army ant colony moves almost incessantly over the time it exists.

q: Where do most salmon go to lay their eggs?
o: The deepest part of the sea
x: Salmon hatch in fresh water, grow up in the sea, then return home to breed. Tracking studies show this is mostly true.
evidence: The adult salmon then return primarily to their natal streams to spawn.

q: European eels from rivers across Europe travel to which sea to spawn?
x: After spawning there, the young drift north through the Atlantic. Wild eel mating has never been seen.
evidence: After spawning in the Sargasso Sea, they disperse northwards throughout the Atlantic Ocean, its coasts, and the rivers that empty into it.

q: What is the timing of the blue wildebeest's long migration linked to?
x: Nutritious grass helps mothers make milk and calves grow. They can run at up to 80 km/h (50 mph).
evidence: Three African populations of blue wildebeest take part in a long-distance migration, timed to coincide with the annual pattern of rainfall and grass growth

q: Which humpback whales sing the famous long, complex songs?
x: A song typically lasts from 4 to 33 minutes.
evidence: Males produce a complex song that typically lasts from 4 to 33 minutes.

q: How do humpback whales often trap krill and small fish?
x: A group swims in a shrinking circle blowing bubbles, trapping prey in a bubble cylinder. It counts as tool use.
evidence: Humpbacks typically hunt their prey with bubble nets, which is considered to be a form of tool use.

q: Each of a humpback whale's flippers is about how long compared with its body?
x: Its genus name, Megaptera, means "giant wing", after these huge flippers.
evidence: The species has a bulky body with a thin rostrum and proportionally long flippers, each around one-third of its body length.

q: The orca, or killer whale, is the largest member of which family?
x: Orcas live in close family groups called pods, and each group has its own hunting tricks and calls.
evidence: The orca (Orcinus orca), or killer whale, is a toothed whale and the largest member of the oceanic dolphin family.

q: Why did orcas get the name "killer whales"?
a: Sailors saw them hunt larger whales
x: Orcas hunt many prey, including fish, sharks, rays, seals, dolphins and whales.
evidence: Orcas are often referred to as "killer whales" because ancient sailors saw them hunt larger whales.

q: Why do most fireflies flash their lights at twilight?
x: Fireflies are actually beetles. The glow probably started as a warning that the larvae taste bad.
evidence: They are soft-bodied beetles commonly called fireflies, lightning bugs, or glowworms for their conspicuous emission of light, mainly during twilight, to attract mates.

q: Why do female Photuris fireflies copy the flash patterns of another firefly kind?
a: To lure males and eat them
x: These "femme fatale" fireflies trap males of the Photinus genus as prey.
evidence: adult female fireflies of the genus Photuris mimic the flash pattern of the Photinus beetle to trap their males as prey.

q: How does the archerfish catch insects sitting above the water?
a: It spits jets of water at them
o: It waits for them to drown
x: An adult almost always hits on the first shot and can knock down prey up to 3 m (10 ft) above the surface.
evidence: are a family of percomorph tropical fish known for their unique predation technique of "shooting down" land-based insects and other small prey with jets of water spit from their specialized mouths.

q: What does the cleaner wrasse do for bigger fish at its "cleaning stations"?
x: Cleaners even swim into the open mouths and gills of predatory fish to do their job.
evidence: "Client" fish congregate at wrasse "cleaning stations" and wait for the cleaner fish to remove gnathiid parasites, the cleaners even swimming into their open mouths and gill cavities to do so.

q: Clownfish rely on which animals for shelter and protection?
x: In return, clownfish protect the anemone from fish that eat anemones, and clean and fan it.
evidence: Clownfish developed a symbiotic and mutually beneficial relationship with sea anemones, on which they rely for shelter and protection from predators.

q: In a clownfish group, what happens when the breeding female disappears?
x: The others then move up the size ranking, and the largest non-breeder becomes the new breeding male.
evidence: When the female disappears, the breeding male changes sex and takes her place while the others move up the hierarchy.

q: A remora's sucker disc, which grips onto sharks, is a changed form of which body part?
x: Sliding backwards makes the suction stronger, and swimming forward releases it. Remoras sometimes stick to divers.
evidence: Their distinctive first dorsal fins take the form of a modified oval, sucker-like organ with slat-like structures that open and close to create suction and take a firm hold against the skin of larger marine animals.

q: Why do hermit crabs live inside empty snail shells?
x: Their abdomen is soft, so without a borrowed shell they would be defenceless.
evidence: Hermit crabs are anomuran decapod crustaceans of the superfamily Paguroidea that have adapted to occupy empty scavenged gastropod shells to protect their fragile abdomens.

q: About how much of a male superb lyrebird's song is copied from other animals?
x: It mostly copies other birds, sometimes marsupials. It lives in forests of southeastern Australia.
evidence: The superb lyrebird is renowned for its elaborate vocal mimicry, with an estimated 70–80% of the male's vocalisations consisting of imitations of other species, mostly other birds but occasionally marsupials.

q: What helps keep an Arctic fox's feet warm on snow and ice?
a: Fur on the soles of its feet
o: Extra blood flow to its feet
x: It also has reduced blood flow to its legs and keeps its paw temperature separate from its core.
evidence: Foxes also have fur on the soles of their feet and reduced blood flow to their legs to help keep them warm.

q: How does an Arctic fox's coat change through the year?
a: Darker in summer, lighter in winter
o: Lighter in summer, darker in winter
x: It sheds twice a year. The thick winter coat helps hide it against snow and keeps it warm.
evidence: Arctic foxes shed twice a year, switching between their summer coat, which is darker, and their winter coat, which is lighter.

q: Dung beetles are the only insects known to find their way using what?
x: They can still navigate when only the Milky Way or clusters of bright stars are visible.
evidence: Dung beetles can also navigate when only the Milky Way or clusters of bright stars are visible, making them the only insects known to orient themselves by the Milky Way.

q: A male dung beetle of the species Onthophagus taurus can pull about how many times its own weight?
x: That is like an average person pulling six double-decker buses full of people.
evidence: male Onthophagus taurus can pull 1,141 times their own body weight, the equivalent of an average person pulling six double-decker buses full of people.

q: Why is the green sea turtle called "green"?
x: The green fat comes from its diet of seagrass. Its shell is actually olive to black.
evidence: The common name refers to the usually green fat found beneath its carapace, due to its diet strictly being seagrass, not to the color of its carapace, which is olive to black.

q: What do adult green sea turtles mostly eat?
x: It is the only sea turtle that is herbivorous when fully grown.
evidence: The green sea turtle is the only aquatic turtle species which is herbivorous when fully grown.

q: What does the marine iguana go into the sea to eat?
x: It is the only modern lizard that forages in the sea. Big males dive for food, while others feed at low tide.
evidence: Unique among modern lizards, it is a marine reptile that has the ability to forage in the sea for algae, which make up almost all of its diet.

q: The marine iguana, the only lizard that forages in the sea, lives only where?
x: The Galápagos Islands belong to Ecuador. Marine iguanas live in colonies on rocky shores.
evidence: is a species of iguana found only on the Galápagos Islands (Ecuador).

q: During El Niño years when food is scarce, some marine iguanas can do what?
x: They grow back when food returns. Scientists think their bones may actually shorten.
evidence: During an El Niño cycle in which food diminished for two years, some were found to decrease their length by as much as 20%.

q: Why is the common basilisk nicknamed the "Jesus Christ lizard"?
x: It runs upright on its hind legs. It can also stay underwater for up to half an hour.
evidence: It is also known as the Jesus Christ lizard, Jesus lizard, South American Jesus lizard, or lagarto de Jesus Cristo for its ability to run on the surface of water.

q: Why do flying fish leap out of the water and glide?
x: Their wing-like fins let them glide far. Underwater hunters include tuna, swordfish and marlin.
evidence: The main reason for this behavior is thought to be to escape from underwater predators, which include swordfish, mackerel, tuna, and marlin, among others

q: How does the wood frog survive freezing winters?
o: It swims under the ice all winter
It digs below the frost line
x: Sugar and urea in its tissues work like antifreeze to limit the ice. It is the only North American frog north of the Arctic Circle.
evidence: Similar to other northern frogs that enter dormancy close to the surface in soil and/or leaf litter, wood frogs can tolerate the freezing of their blood and other tissues.

q: What does the common vampire bat feed on?
x: It favours horses and cattle. Its saliva has a substance that stops blood clotting, named Draculin.
evidence: The common vampire bat practices hematophagy, mainly feeding on the blood of livestock.

q: What helps a vampire bat find blood vessels near the skin?
x: It usually picks the rump, flank or neck, then laps up blood with a grooved tongue.
evidence: heat sensors in the nose help it to detect blood vessels near the surface of the skin.

q: How do vampire bats often help roost mates who are hungry?
x: Sharing depends on being related, being friends and past help. Bats that groom each other also share food.
evidence: Regurgitated food sharing in common vampire bats has been studied in both the lab and field, and is predicted by kinship, association, and reciprocal help.

q: Who is in charge in a spotted hyena clan?
x: Spotted hyena society is matriarchal. Females are larger than males and dominate them.
evidence: Spotted hyena society is matriarchal; females are larger than males and dominate them.

q: How does the spotted hyena mainly get its food?
x: It also scavenges and can digest skin and bone. It hunts alone, in small parties or in large groups.
evidence: it is primarily a hunter but may also scavenge, with the capacity to eat and digest skin, bone and other animal waste.

q: What makes up almost the whole diet of the giant panda?
x: Although it belongs to the order Carnivora, the panda is mostly herbivorous.
evidence: It can digest starch and is mostly herbivorous with a diet consisting almost entirely of bamboo and bamboo shoots.

q: About how much bamboo does an average giant panda eat each day?
x: Bamboo has little energy, so pandas must eat a lot of it.
evidence: The average giant panda eats 9 to 14 kg (20 to 31 lb) of bamboo shoots per day to compensate for the limited energy content of its diet.

q: In which country do wild giant pandas live?
x: They live in six mountain regions, mainly in Sichuan, and also Shaanxi and Gansu.
evidence: It is found in small, fragmented populations in six mountainous regions in the country, mainly in Sichuan, and also in neighbouring Shaanxi and Gansu.

q: What helps a giant panda hold bamboo while it eats?
a: A thumb-like part of its paw
x: An average panda eats 9 to 14 kg of bamboo a day, so a good grip matters.
evidence: A thumb is visible on its forepaw, which helps in holding bamboo in place for feeding.

q: How does the bombardier beetle defend itself when disturbed?
x: A chemical reaction heats the spray to near boiling and shoots it out with a popping sound.
evidence: when disturbed, they eject a hot, noxious chemical spray from their pygidial glands with a popping sound.

q: Where does the frilled lizard spend over 90% of each day?
x: It comes down mostly to feed, meet others or move to a new tree. It lives in northern Australia and southern New Guinea.
evidence: The frilled lizard is a diurnal (daytime) and arboreal species, spending over 90% each day up in the trees.

q: A peacock's famous long "train" is made of which feathers?
x: These covert feathers have colourful eyespots and are raised into a fan for courtship. He can still fly.
evidence: The train is made up of elongated upper-tail covert feathers with colourful eyespots.

q: What do Adélie penguins build their nests from?
x: Adélie penguins live all around the coast of Antarctica and eat mainly krill and fish.
evidence: Adélies build rough nests of stones.

q: Wild orangutans are now found only on which two islands?
x: Long ago they lived across Southeast Asia and South China.
