evidence: They are now found only in parts of Borneo and Sumatra, but during the Pleistocene they ranged throughout Southeast Asia and South China.

q: Which is the most solitary of the great apes?
x: Social bonds are mainly between mothers and their young. Orangutans are also the most tree-living great apes.
evidence: Orangutans are the most solitary of the great apes: social bonds occur primarily between mothers and their dependent offspring.

q: What is the most important part of an orangutan's diet?
x: They also eat leaves, bark, honey, insects and bird eggs, and they build a new sleeping nest every night.
evidence: Fruit is the most important component of an orangutan's diet, but they will also eat vegetation, bark, honey, insects and bird eggs.

q: Japanese macaques, or snow monkeys, are famous for which winter habit?
x: They also roll snowballs for fun. Some live where snow covers the ground for months.
evidence: The macaque has other unusual behaviours, including bathing together in hot springs and rolling snowballs for fun.

q: On Koshima Island, a young macaque called Imo began a habit that spread through her troop. What was it?
x: Imo washed sweet potatoes, then even dipped them in salty seawater. The habit passed down the generations.
evidence: witnessed one female, named Imo (Japanese for yam or potato), washing the food off with river water rather than brushing it off as the others were doing

q: What helps a honey badger twist around freely, even when grabbed?
x: Thick skin, strength and fierce defence mean it has few natural predators.
evidence: It has a fairly long body, with a distinctly thick-set and broad back, and remarkably loose skin, allowing the badger to turn and twist freely within it.

q: How does the secretarybird often kill its prey?
o: By diving from high in the sky
x: This tall bird of prey hunts on foot in African grasslands, standing up to 1.3 m (4 ft 3 in) tall.
evidence: The secretarybird hunts and catches prey on the ground, often stomping on victims to kill them.

q: What do honeypot ant "repletes" do for their colony?
a: Store food in their swollen bodies
x: They act as living pantries, sharing the stored food when food is scarce.
evidence: Honey ants are unique in using their own bodies as living storage, used later by their fellow ants when food is otherwise scarce.

q: About how much of a brown bear's diet comes from plants?
x: It is an omnivore, but in parts of coastal Alaska it feeds mainly on spawning salmon.
evidence: Contrary to popular belief, the brown bear derives 90% of its diet from plants.

q: What protects mongooses against snake venom?
x: Venom toxins cannot bind to their modified receptors. At least four groups of mammals have this protection.
evidence: Mongooses are one of at least four known mammalian taxa with mutations in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor that protect against snake venom.

q: If a hognose snake playing dead is turned right side up, what does it often do?
x: First it hisses and spreads its neck like a cobra. Even while "dead", it keeps watching the threat.
evidence: If they are rolled upright while in this state, they will often roll back as if insisting they really are dead.

q: An ant queen can live for up to about how long?
x: Worker ants usually live only 1 to 3 years.
evidence: The queens can live for up to 30 years, and workers live from 1 to 3 years.

q: What do some ants, such as fire ants, do to survive floods?
o: Ride on the backs of birds
x: These rafts may also help ants reach and settle new islands.
evidence: Some species also form floating rafts that help them survive floods.

q: Which of these places has no native ants?
x: Ants live on every continent except Antarctica. Greenland and Hawaii also lack native ants.
evidence: They are found on all continents except Antarctica, and only a few large islands, such as Greenland, Iceland, parts of Polynesia and the Hawaiian Islands lack native ant species.

q: Wild lemurs live only on which island?
x: Over a dozen kinds of giant lemurs, some as big as gorillas, died out after humans reached the island.
evidence: They are endemic to the island of Madagascar.

q: Which is the world's only flightless parrot?
x: It is also the heaviest parrot, comes out at night, and may live up to 100 years. It lives only in New Zealand.
evidence: It is the world's only flightless parrot, the world's heaviest parrot, and also is nocturnal, herbivorous, visibly sexually dimorphic in body size, has a low basal metabolic rate, and does not have male parental care.

q: Polar bears live in the Arctic. Where do wild penguins live?
a: Almost all in the Southern Hemisphere
x: Only one species, the Galápagos penguin, lives at and slightly north of the equator.
evidence: Penguins are a group of flightless semi-aquatic sea birds which live almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere.

q: Which is the only penguin found north of the equator?
x: It is adapted to the warm equatorial climate and is the only penguin that moults twice a year.
evidence: It is the only penguin found north of the equator.

q: The okapi, or "forest giraffe", lives wild only in which country?
x: It lives in the northeast of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Europeans once called it the "African unicorn".
evidence: is an artiodactyl mammal that is endemic to the northeast Democratic Republic of the Congo.

q: The okapi has zebra-like stripes, but which animal is its closest relative?
x: The okapi and the giraffe are the only living members of the giraffe family.
evidence: Although it has striped markings reminiscent of zebras, it is most closely related to the giraffe.

q: Snow leopards live in which kind of habitat?
x: They live at 3,000 to 4,500 m (9,800 to 14,800 ft), from the Himalayas to Mongolia. Thick tails help them in the cold.
evidence: The snow leopard is native to the mountain ranges of Asia, ranging from eastern Hindu Kush, the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau to southern Siberia, Mongolia and western China.

q: Llamas have been used as pack animals for centuries by the peoples of which mountains?
x: The llama is a domesticated South American camelid. It can carry about 25 to 30% of its body weight.
evidence: is a domesticated South American camelid, widely used as a meat and pack animal by Andean cultures since the pre-Columbian era.

q: What is the biggest cat species in the Americas?
x: It is the third-largest cat in the world and lives from the southwestern United States to northern Argentina.
evidence: it is the biggest cat species in the Americas and the third largest in the world.

q: The Tasmanian devil once lived across mainland Australia. Where is its natural home today?
x: It died out on the mainland about 3,500 years ago. It is the size of a small dog with a very strong bite.
evidence: It was formerly present across mainland Australia, but became extinct there around 3,500 years ago; it is now confined to the island of Tasmania.

q: Which animal became the largest meat-eating marsupial after the thylacine died out in 1936?
x: For its size, the devil has one of the strongest bites of any land predator.
evidence: The size of a small dog, the Tasmanian devil became the largest carnivorous marsupial in the world following the extinction of the thylacine in 1936.

q: What is the largest living species of tortoise?
x: It can weigh up to 417 kg (919 lb) and often lives more than 100 years in the wild.
evidence: It is the largest living species of tortoise, and can weigh up to 417 kg (919 lb).

q: The Galápagos Islands were named after which animal?
x: Spanish explorers named the islands after the Spanish word galápago, meaning "tortoise".
evidence: Spanish explorers, who discovered the islands in the 16th century, named them after the Spanish galápago, meaning "tortoise".

q: Rottnest Island, home of many quokkas, means "rat nest island". Why?
a: An explorer thought they were giant rats
o: The island was full of rats
Rats came there on Dutch ships
x: Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh named it in 1696. Quokkas live only in a small part of southwestern Australia.
evidence: In 1696, Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh mistook them for giant rats, and renamed the Wadjemup Island 't Eylandt 't Rottenest, which means "the rat nest island" in Dutch.

q: Over half of the diet of the fossa, Madagascar's largest carnivore, is made of which animals?
x: The fossa looks a bit like a small cougar. It also eats tenrecs, rodents, lizards and birds.
evidence: Over 50% of its diet consists of lemurs, the endemic primates found on the island; tenrecs, rodents, lizards, birds, and other animals are also documented as prey.

q: Where does the red panda live in the wild?
x: It lives in mountain forests with lots of bamboo. Despite its name, it is not closely related to the giant panda.
evidence: The red panda (Ailurus fulgens), also known as the lesser panda, is a small mammal native to the eastern Himalayas and southwestern China.

q: Why is the beluga whale nicknamed the "sea canary"?
o: It lives near the Canary Islands
x: Belugas live in the Arctic. Having no dorsal fin helps them swim under the ice.
evidence: It is also known as the sea canary, due to its high-pitched calls

q: The walrus's scientific name comes from Greek for "tooth walk". Why?
a: It uses its tusks to haul itself out
o: It walks on its teeth on land
Its teeth chatter as it walks
It grows teeth on its flippers
x: Walruses were seen using their tusks to pull themselves out of the water onto ice.
evidence: The compound Odobenus comes from odous (Greek for 'teeth') and baino (Greek for 'walk'), based on observations of walruses using their tusks to pull themselves out of the water.

q: What do walruses mostly search the shallow sea floor for?
x: Walruses live in the Arctic and spend much time on sea ice. Big males can weigh over 2,000 kg (4,400 lb).
evidence: Walrus live mostly in shallow waters above the continental shelves, spending significant amounts of their lives on the sea ice looking for benthic bivalve molluscs.

q: The proboscis monkey, famous for its huge nose, lives only on which island?
x: It lives mostly in mangrove forests and coastal areas. A male's nose can be over 10 cm (4 in) long.
evidence: It is endemic to the Southeast Asian island of Borneo and is found mostly in mangrove forests and on the coastal areas of the island.

q: Bonobos and chimpanzees are separated by the Congo River. Which side do bonobos live on?
x: Neither ape swims well, so the river probably kept the two species apart for a very long time.
evidence: Bonobos live south of the river, and thereby were separated from the ancestors of the common chimpanzee, which live north of the river.

q: Gelada monkeys are found only in the highlands of which country?
x: Males have a bright red hourglass-shaped patch on the chest, giving the nickname "bleeding-heart monkey".
evidence: is a species of Old World monkey found only in the Ethiopian Highlands, living at elevations of 1,800–4,400 m (5,900–14,400 ft) above sea level.

q: Despite its scary name, what does the vampire squid eat?
x: Its name comes from its dark colour and cloak-like webbing. It lives in the deep sea.
evidence: The name Vampyroteuthis was reportedly inspired by its dark colour and cloaklike webbing, rather than its habits — it feeds on detritus, not blood.

q: Giant tube worms live in big clusters around what?
x: They can grow up to 3 m (9 ft 10 in) long and were first found in 1977 on the Galápagos Rift.
evidence: Riftia worms are sessile and are found clustered together in large colonies around deep-sea hydrothermal vents in the East Pacific Rise and the Galapagos Rift.

q: How do adult giant tube worms get energy, since they have no gut?
x: The bacteria use chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide from the vents to make food.
evidence: Adult Riftia worms lack a digestive system and rely on their symbiotic relationship with chemotrophic sulfur-oxidising bacteria to provide them with energy.

q: Where does the blind, pale salamander called the olm live?
x: It lives in caves of southeastern Europe. People once thought olms washed out by rain were baby cave dragons.
evidence: Living in caves found in the Dinaric Alps, the genus is endemic to the waters that flow underground through the extensive limestone bedrock of the karst of Central and Southeastern Europe

q: The fennec fox lives in which kind of habitat?
x: It is the smallest fox. Its coat, ears and kidneys are all adapted to heat and little water.
evidence: The fennec fox (Vulpes zerda) is a small fox native to the deserts of North Africa, ranging from Western Sahara and Mauritania to the Sinai Peninsula.

q: What are the fennec fox's huge ears for?
x: It listens for prey moving underground. Fennec families dig big burrows in the sand.
evidence: Its most distinctive feature is its unusually large ears, which serve to dissipate heat and listen for underground prey.

q: How does the thorny devil, an Australian desert lizard, drink?
a: Skin grooves carry water to its mouth
o: It sucks water up through its feet
x: Touching water with any part of its body is enough. It even shovels damp sand onto its back.
evidence: The thorny devil's scales are ridged, enabling the animal to collect water by simply touching it with any part of the body, usually the limbs; capillary action transports the water to the mouth through channels in its skin.

q: What unusual feature do young hoatzin chicks have?
x: The claws help chicks climb branches. If they fall into the water, they swim and climb back up.
evidence: Hoatzin chicks have two claws on each wing.

q: What does most of the hoatzin's diet consist of?
x: One study found its diet was 82% leaves. It ferments plant food in its gut a bit like a cow.
evidence: One study, undertaken in Venezuela, found that the hoatzin's diet was 82% leaves, 10% flowers, and 8% fruit.

q: Poison dart frogs are native to which region?
x: Their bright colours warn predators that they are toxic. The poison comes from eating ants, mites and termites.
evidence: is the common name of a group of frogs in the family Dendrobatinae which are native to tropical Central and South America.

q: Piranhas are often said to eat only meat. What is their real diet?
x: Diets vary a lot between species. All piranhas have a single row of sharp, interlocking teeth.
evidence: Although often described as extremely predatory and mainly feeding on fish, their dietary habits vary extensively, and they will also take plant material, leading to their classification as omnivorous.

q: Where does the pink river dolphin, or boto, live?
x: It lives in the Amazon and Orinoco basins and the upper Madeira River in Bolivia.
evidence: The Amazon river dolphin (Inia geoffrensis), also known as the boto, bufeo or pink river dolphin, is a species of toothed whale endemic to South America

q: The coelacanth was thought extinct for 66 million years. Off which country was a living one fished in 1938?
x: They also live around the Comoro Islands, and a second species was found in Indonesia in the late 1990s.
evidence: was described from specimens fished off the coast of South Africa from 1938 onward; they are now also known to inhabit the seas around the Comoro Islands off the east coast of Africa.

q: The Baikal seal lives only in fresh water, in a lake in which country?
x: It lives only in Lake Baikal in Siberia and has been there for about two million years.
evidence: is a species of earless seal endemic to Lake Baikal in Siberia, Russia.

q: Which feature lets you tell a dugong apart from a manatee?
x: Manatees have rounded, paddle-like tails. The dugong grazes on seagrass meadows in the Indo-West Pacific.
evidence: The dugong is easily distinguishable from the manatees by its fluked, dolphin-like tail; it also possesses a unique skull and teeth.

q: The saola, or "Asian unicorn", lives in the forests of which countries?
x: It was discovered in 1992 and is so rare that the last record was a camera photo in 2013.
evidence: is a forest-dwelling bovid native to the Annamite Range in Vietnam and Laos.

q: The vaquita, the smallest cetacean, lives only in which body of water?
x: It has the smallest range of any whale, dolphin or porpoise, in Mexican waters.
evidence: is a species of porpoise endemic to the northern end of the Gulf of California in Baja California, Mexico.

q: How does the American pika prepare for winter?
o: It digs up roots each day
x: This is called haying. The pika is a small relative of rabbits that lives on rocky mountain slopes.
evidence: gathering and storing plant materials in "haypiles" to sustain itself through the winter months, a behavior known as haying.

q: The kea is a parrot that lives in which unusual habitat?
x: Kea live in forests and alpine areas of New Zealand's South Island, and are famous for their intelligence.
evidence: is a species of large parrot in the family Strigopidae that is endemic to the forested and alpine regions of the South Island of New Zealand.

q: Where does the shoebill, a stork-like bird with a huge bill, live?
x: It lives in large swamps from South Sudan to Zambia, often where papyrus and lungfish are found.
evidence: It lives in tropical East Africa in large swamps from South Sudan down to Zambia.

q: What makes a southern cassowary's feet dangerous?
a: A dagger-like claw up to 12 cm
x: The claw is on the inner of its three toes. It also has a horn-like casque on its head.
evidence: The three-toed feet are thick and powerful, equipped with a dagger-like claw up to 12 cm (4.7 in) on the inner toe.

q: Southern cassowaries live in New Guinea and which other country?
x: They are found in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and northeastern Australia.
evidence: is a large, flightless, mostly black bird, found in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and northeastern Australia.

q: Why does a wombat's pouch open backwards?
a: To keep dirt out while it digs
o: So the baby can see behind
x: Wombats dig big burrows with strong claws and ever-growing, rodent-like front teeth.
evidence: The advantage of a backward-facing pouch is that when digging, the wombat does not gather soil in its pouch over its young.

q: What is unusual about wombat droppings?
x: Research into how wombats make cubes won an Ig Nobel Prize for Physics in 2019.
evidence: Wombats leave distinctive cube-shaped faeces.

q: What does a camel's hump store?
x: Storing water in the hump is a myth. Using the fat as energy also makes water inside the body.
evidence: It is a common myth that a camel stores water in its hump, but the humps in fact are reservoirs of fatty tissue, which can be used as a reserve source of calories, not water.

q: How do camels keep sand out of their eyes in desert storms?
x: Bushy eyebrows help too, and camels can close their nostrils to keep sand out.
evidence: The bushy eyebrows and the double row of eyelashes prevent sand and dust from entering the eyes during strong windstorms, and shield them from the sun's glare.

q: The two-humped Bactrian camel is native to which region?
x: The wild Bactrian camel is a separate species and the only truly wild camel of the Old World.
evidence: is a camel native to the steppes of Central Asia.

q: What are an echidna's spines made of?
x: The spines are modified hairs. Echidnas live in Australia and New Guinea and, like the platypus, lay eggs.
evidence: The spines are modified hairs and are made of keratin, the same fibrous protein that makes up fur, claws, nails, and horn sheaths.

q: The aardvark, a burrowing ant-eater, is native to which continent?
x: Its name means "earth pig". It digs ants and termites out of their mounds at night.
evidence: is a medium-sized, burrowing, nocturnal mammal native to Africa.

q: What does the aardvark eat?
x: It uses sharp claws to dig into insect mounds and its long snout to sniff out food.
evidence: A nocturnal feeder, the aardvark subsists on ants and termites (myrmecophagy) by using its sharp claws and powerful legs to dig the insects out of their hills, and its long snout to sniff out food.

q: The numbat of Western Australia eats almost nothing but what?
x: Unlike most marsupials, the numbat is active by day. It is the animal emblem of Western Australia.
evidence: It is diurnal and its diet consists almost exclusively of termites.

q: Which bird is the only known vertebrate whose diet is 70 to 90% bone?
x: Its old name "ossifrage" means "bone-breaker" in Latin.
evidence: The bearded vulture is the only known vertebrate whose diet consists of 70–90% bone.

q: How does the Egyptian vulture break open big eggs?
o: It sits on them until they crack
x: Tool use is rare in birds. It also uses twigs to roll up wool for its nest.
evidence: They also feed on the eggs of other birds, breaking larger ones by tossing a large pebble onto them.

q: What is the silkworm's favourite food?
x: Silkworms are the caterpillars of the domestic silk moth and are famous for making silk.
evidence: The silkworm's preferred food are the leaves of white mulberry, though they may eat other species of mulberry, and even leaves of other plants.

q: What does the king cobra mainly hunt?
x: It even eats other king cobras. Lizards and rodents are only occasional prey.
evidence: It chiefly hunts other snakes, including those of its own kind, although other lizards and rodents are also occasional prey.

q: What is the world's longest venomous snake?
x: It averages 3.18 to 4 m (10.4 to 13.1 ft), with a record of 5.85 m (19.2 ft).
evidence: With an average length of 3.18 to 4 m (10.4 to 13.1 ft) and a record length of 5.85 m (19.2 ft), it is the world's longest venomous snake and among the heaviest.

q: What does a female king cobra build that no other snake builds?
a: An above-ground nest for her eggs
o: A silk web for her eggs
x: She gathers material for the nest and guards the eggs throughout incubation.
evidence: This is the only ophidian that constructs an above-ground nest for its eggs, which are purposefully and meticulously gathered and protected by the female throughout the incubation period.

q: Which birds are a favourite prey of the leopard seal?
x: This Antarctic hunter also eats other seals, squid, krill and fish. Its teeth are about 2.5 cm (1 in) long.
evidence: It feeds on a wide range of prey including its fellow pinnipeds, cephalopods, krill, fish, and birds, particularly penguins.

q: What helps the osprey grip slippery fish?
a: Its outer toe can turn backwards
x: Ospreys and owls are the only raptors with a reversible outer toe, so they can hold prey with two toes in front and two behind.
evidence: The osprey and owls are the only raptors whose outer toes are reversible, allowing them to grasp their prey with two toes in front and two behind.

q: Manta rays have one of the highest what of any fish?
x: They are filter feeders that eat zooplankton. The biggest species can be 7 m (23 ft) across.
evidence: They have one of the highest brain-to-body ratio of all fish, advanced cognition, and may understand mirror contingencies.

q: Which mosquitoes drink blood?
x: All mosquitoes drink nectar. Some females need a blood meal before they can make eggs.
evidence: All mosquitoes drink nectar from flowers; females of many species have adapted to also drink blood.

q: How does a cone snail catch its prey?
x: The barbed tooth shoots out on the end of its proboscis. Stings from some big cone snails can kill humans.
evidence: The tooth, which is likened to a dart or a harpoon, is barbed and can be extended some distance out from the head of the snail at the end of the proboscis.

q: What do crossbills use their crossed beak tips for?
a: Getting seeds out of pine cones
x: The red crossbill is a small finch. Its mandibles cross at the tips to pry open conifer cones.
evidence: Crossbills have distinctive mandibles, crossed at the tips, which enable them to extract seeds from conifer cones and other fruits.
